source.title: Are Textual Residuals Truly Complementary? Learning Visual Complements under Semantic Superposition for Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
source.authors: Xiao-Yang Li; Ming-Ming Lu; Wei-Zhen Zhou; Hao Li; Can-Hui Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, through the references. There are minor extraction artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the relevant results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses semantic superposition as motivation for a task-specific residual-selection and calibration method. Its measurements concern the learned dictionary and residuals produced by that method, not whether an unconstrained network naturally develops superposition under capacity pressure.
record.gate_note: The paper measures concentration of controlled text-edit changes in its sparse feature-strength representation and overlap in its learned dictionary/residuals. These are method-specific measurements, not tests of the natural emergence of superposition, a sparsity-dependent transition, or feature importance. Retrieval and complementarity results are not rows because they measure the performance of the proposed method rather than superposition itself.
record.test_reason: The paper invokes semantic superposition (citing Toy Models and SAE work) only as motivation for a VI-ReID residual method. Its measurements concern its own trained sparse dictionary: change concentration under text edits, coherence and active interference. It never measures whether CLIP text embeddings or any network store features in superposition, whether neurons are polysemantic, or whether dictionary features are canonical units. Dense-vs-sparse concentration (Table 9) shows only that Top-k coding concentrates differences, which follows from the coding constraint. It is not evidence about the encoder's native representation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors conclude that textual residuals are not inherently visual complements and should be selectively represented (sparse, low-interference) and calibrated against identity-level RGB–IR discrepancies. They treat superposition as an assumed motivation, not a tested result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original toy-model method. It trains a shared overcomplete dictionary and sparse feature-strength encoder for text-assisted visible-infrared person re-identification, with coherence/interference regularization and visual-complement calibration.
record.method_sensitivity: The representation concentration varies across controlled text edits. The reported analyses use different representation forms (Dense, FS, Sparse FS) and compare LISR with and without low-interference regularization; no uncertainty is reported for these mechanism measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-k sparse feature-strength differences put 94.48% of change magnitude in 64 coordinates, versus 13.45% for dense CLIP differences, across ten single-attribute text edits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-k sparse coding of text embeddings concentrates single-attribute edit differences into few coordinates; this is partly forced by the k=64 budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Coherence regularization lowers mean dictionary coherence by 19.2%, but active interference by only 0.9%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Global dictionary decorrelation in a task-trained SAE need not proportionally reduce activation-weighted interference.

record.code_released: Code and implementation details will be released upon publication.
record.problems: The geometric and concentration measurements concern a deliberately trained sparse dictionary and do not establish how an unmodified network represents features. The controlled text-edit analysis uses ten edit pairs; uncertainty estimates for the reported mechanism measurements are not stated. The paper says statistical significance is not established for some ablation gains.
record.rows_left_out: Retrieval results, complementarity metrics, robustness comparisons, and ablations of residual construction/calibration were left out because they report the proposed method's task performance or residual utility, not direct measurements of the claim's representation geometry. Table 3 and Tables 4–8, 11–12; Secs. 5.3–5.7.

untested.parts: No toy model, sparsity-dependent transition, or geometry of naturally learned features.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity/importance allocation.
Its dictionary is trained on CLIP text embeddings, but it reports no interpretability or feature-recovery result showing sparse features exist in the model.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity. The authors disclaim a one-to-one mapping between dictionary directions and concepts.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Toy Models of Superposition only as motivation; it is not one of the original sources' tests. The concentration result is largely by construction: C256 = 100% follows from k = 64, as the authors note. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test natural feature storage under capacity pressure, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry in toy networks; it measures a trained dictionary used by its method.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared capacity.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Does not measure feature distribution across LLM neurons or recover LLM features with an SAE.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; it states that its learned dictionary directions need not correspond one-to-one with semantic concepts.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features or test which dimensionality carries a model feature.

relation.reason: Operationalizes the superposition motivation through sparse coding and interference suppression, without measuring whether the original text representations exhibit superposition.

tranche.reason: Uses superposition to motivate sparse residual construction and evaluates its own retrieval method and regularized dictionary, without testing a catalog claim version.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Both rows describe method ablations; their versions=none and cannot_determine states are appropriate, and they provide no independent evidence for a superposition claim.

statements.correction: Tri-SYSU-MM01, Full LISR versus w/o Low-Interference: Coh 0.01837 → 0.01485 (−19.2%); AI 0.04744 → 0.04701 (−0.9%). Comparison includes Lcoh and Lint.
statements.problem: The percentages are correct, but Table 10 compares full low-interference learning against its removal; it does not isolate coherence regularization alone. Low-interference learning includes dictionary coherence and activation-dependent interference penalties.
